mcqs.question: Why is a stack the natural structure for validating nested brackets like `([{}])`?
options: A hash map counting each bracket type is simpler and equally correct
Brackets always appear in pairs, so any structure would work
Nesting requires the most recently opened structure to be the first closed, which is exactly the LIFO order a stack enforces
A queue naturally tracks which bracket opened first
mcqs.explanation: Valid nesting means the innermost still-open structure must close first — a stack's push-on-open, match-against-top-on-close behavior enforces exactly that ordering. A count-based approach can't detect wrong order (like `)(`), and a queue would check the oldest open bracket first, which is the wrong end for this problem.

mcqs.question: Why does comparing `s.count('(') == s.count(')')` fail to validate balanced parentheses correctly?
options: It correctly validates single-bracket-type strings but is slower than a stack
It works correctly for all cases including mixed bracket types
Count comparison only fails on empty strings
It only checks that counts match, missing both ordering (`)(` has equal counts but is invalid) and type-matching for mixed brackets
mcqs.explanation: Equal counts is a necessary but nowhere near sufficient condition — `")("` has one of each and is clearly invalid, and the approach has no way to represent multiple bracket types matching correctly at all. It isn't merely slower than the correct approach; it's outright wrong for cases a stack handles correctly, including well beyond just empty-string edge cases.

mcqs.question: The brute-force next-greater-element solution scans rightward from every index independently. What inefficiency does a smarter, stack-based approach eliminate?
options: It avoids repeating the rightward scan for indices whose answer could be inferred from work already done for earlier or later indices
It eliminates the need to know each element's value
It reduces the problem to sorting the array first
It removes the need to track direction (left-to-right vs right-to-left)
mcqs.explanation: Brute force reruns an independent scan per index even though a later, bigger element often answers the next-greater question for several earlier elements at once — a fact the stack-based approach exploits to do the whole problem in one O(n) pass instead of O(n²). It doesn't require sorting, and element values and scan direction still matter in the optimized version.

mcqs.question: In the shunting-yard infix-to-postfix algorithm, why does an incoming operator only get pushed onto the operator stack after popping everything on top with equal or higher precedence?
options: So numbers are always output before any operator
Because the operators being popped bind at least as tightly and must be resolved before the new, less-tightly-binding operator can be applied, preserving correct precedence in the output order
To detect mismatched parentheses
Because the operator stack has a fixed maximum size
mcqs.explanation: Postfix order encodes evaluation order directly, so any operator that binds at least as tightly as the incoming one must appear earlier in the output — popping it first guarantees that. Numbers going to output first is a separate rule handled elsewhere in the algorithm, and this popping step isn't related to parenthesis matching or any stack size limit.

mcqs.question: Converting `"3 - 4 - 5"` to postfix using `>` instead of `>=` when popping equal-precedence operators produces a wrong result. Why?
options: Because subtraction isn't supported by shunting-yard
Because the expression has too many numbers
Because `>` never pops equal-precedence operators already on the stack, changing the grouping and breaking left-associativity
Because parentheses are missing from the expression
mcqs.explanation: Left-associative operators like subtraction must be popped when the incoming operator has equal precedence, which requires `>=`; using strict `>` leaves an equal-precedence operator sitting on the stack, silently reordering the computation away from left-to-right grouping. The issue is purely the comparison operator's strictness, not the absence of parentheses or a limit on operand count.

mcqs.question: When would you prefer an explicit stack over recursive-descent parsing for evaluating a nested expression?
options: Always — recursion can never correctly parse nested parentheses
Never — explicit stacks are strictly slower
Only when the expression contains no parentheses at all
When input can be extremely deeply nested and risks exceeding the language's call-stack recursion limit
mcqs.explanation: Recursive descent handles nesting naturally by using the call stack itself, but that ties depth to the language's recursion limit; pathologically deep nesting can overflow it, while an explicit stack is bounded only by available memory. Recursion parses nested parentheses correctly under normal depth, both approaches have comparable time complexity, and the choice is unrelated to whether parentheses are present at all.
